questions.question: How do you write a Gradle build script for a Spring Boot project?
questions.title: Writing a Gradle Build Script for a Spring Boot Project
questions.direct_answer: A Spring Boot Gradle build script applies the `org.springframework.boot` and `io.spring.dependency-management` plugins, declares dependencies in a `dependencies` block, and uses `bootJar` to produce an executable JAR.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can set up a real Spring Boot project with Gradle from scratch.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not applying the `io.spring.dependency-management` plugin, which means you have to specify versions for every Spring dependency manually instead of inheriting them from the BOM.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Kotlin DSL (`build.gradle.kts`) for type-safe build scripts, the `bootRun` task for local development, and how to customize the executable JAR with `bootJar { archiveFileName = ... }`.

sections.title: Two Plugins That Replace Hundreds of Lines of Build Configuration
sections.content:
Building a Spring Boot application with Gradle requires exactly two plugins, and getting them wrong is the most common setup mistake. The `org.springframework.boot` plugin adds the `bootJar` task that packages your application as an executable fat JAR with an embedded web server, the `bootRun` task for running locally with hot-reload support, and `bootBuildImage` for creating OCI container images. The `io.spring.dependency-management` plugin imports the Spring Boot BOM — a bill of materials that specifies compatible versions for hundreds of libraries so you never specify version numbers for Spring-managed dependencies.

**The mistake most developers make** is omitting the dependency management plugin entirely. Without it, every dependency declaration needs an explicit version number, and those versions must be manually kept compatible with each other. A Jackson 2.16 with a Spring Web 3.1 that expects Jackson 2.15 produces subtle serialization bugs that only surface at runtime. The dependency management plugin eliminates this entire category of problems by ensuring all managed dependencies resolve to versions Spring has tested together.

sections.title: Apply Plugins and Pin the JDK With a Toolchain
Declare Dependencies Without Version Numbers and Customize the Output
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Two plugins are non-negotiable for Spring Boot** — `org.springframework.boot` provides `bootJar`/`bootRun`/`bootBuildImage` tasks, and `io.spring.dependency-management` imports the BOM so no dependency needs an explicit version number
- **`implementation` replaces Maven's compile scope** — keeps dependencies off consumers' compile classpaths, which means faster compilation and no accidental API leakage when building library modules
- **Java toolchain pins the JDK declaratively** — Gradle auto-provisions the correct JDK version, eliminating build failures caused by different `JAVA_HOME` settings across team members and CI agents
- **Layered bootJar optimizes Docker builds** — splits the fat JAR into layers ordered by change frequency so Docker rebuilds reuse cached dependency layers and only rebuild your application classes
- **Version overrides use BOM properties** — `ext['jackson.version'] = '2.17.1'` overrides a managed version without breaking other transitive alignments, unlike manually specifying a version on the dependency coordinate

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Setting up Gradle for a Spring Boot project requires two plugins working together, and a common mistake on either one causes subtle failures that are not obvious from the error messages.

**The two required plugins**
- `org.springframework.boot` provides `bootJar` for packaging an executable fat JAR and `bootRun` for local development; without it you get a standard JAR that does not include Spring Boot's launcher
- `io.spring.dependency-management` imports the Spring Boot BOM, letting you declare `spring-boot-starter-web` without any version number — the BOM ensures all transitive versions are compatible; skipping this plugin means you must version every dependency manually and risk subtle mismatches
- Skipping the dependency management plugin is the most common setup mistake — Jackson and Spring Web can silently use mismatched versions, causing serialization failures that only appear at runtime

**Dependency configuration**
- Use `implementation` for application dependencies — it keeps them internal to the module and avoids leaking transitive dependencies to consumers
- Use `testImplementation` for JUnit, Mockito, AssertJ — they belong only on the test classpath and should never ship in the packaged artifact
- `compileOnly` for Lombok — needed at compile time for annotation processing, not at runtime; the Kotlin equivalent is `kapt`

**Docker-optimized JAR**
- Enable layered `bootJar` with `bootJar { layered { enabled = true } }` — Spring Boot splits the JAR into dependency layer, Spring Boot loader layer, and application class layer; Docker caches the stable layers and only rebuilds the application layer on code changes
- Use the Kotlin DSL for new projects — `build.gradle.kts` provides compile-time type safety and IDE autocomplete in the build script, catching configuration errors before the build runs

questions.question: How does Gradle dependency management work?
questions.title: Gradle Dependency Management Explained
questions.direct_answer: Gradle resolves dependencies from declared repositories (Maven Central, custom Nexus) using configurations (implementation, api, runtimeOnly, testImplementation) and resolves version conflicts by selecting the highest requested version by default, with the option to force or strictly pin specific versions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand dependency configurations, transitive dependency resolution, and conflict resolution strategies.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing `implementation` with `api` — using `api` leaks the dependency into consumers' compile classpaths, creating unnecessary coupling and slower compilation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention dependency constraints, platform BOMs (`platform()`), version catalogs (`libs.versions.toml`), and the dependency insight report (`./gradlew dependencies --configuration compileClasspath`).

sections.title: The Problem: What Breaks When Your Library Leaks Its Internals
sections.content:
Before Gradle introduced the `implementation` and `api` split in version 3.4, every dependency worked like Maven's `compile` scope — visible to everything downstream. If your `service` module depended on Guava internally, every module that depended on `service` could also see and use Guava classes. The moment `service` upgraded Guava or replaced it with a different library, every downstream module broke — even though they had no business using Guava directly.

**This is the dependency leakage problem**, and Gradle's configuration system was redesigned specifically to solve it. The `implementation` configuration makes a dependency available for compilation and runtime within the declaring module, but hides it from any module that depends on yours. The `api` configuration exposes it. The choice between them is not a syntax preference — it determines whether your module's internal dependencies become part of its public contract.

The consequence is practical: a large project using `implementation` everywhere it can compiles faster because Gradle's incremental compiler only reprocesses consumers when the module's public API changes, not when an internal dependency version bumps.

sections.title: Configurations, Conflict Resolution, and the Version Catalog
sections.content:
Gradle organizes dependencies into named **configurations** that map to specific classpaths. `implementation` covers compile and runtime but stays internal. `api` covers compile and runtime and leaks to consumers — use it only in library modules where your public types expose the dependency's types. `runtimeOnly` mirrors Maven's `runtime` scope for things like JDBC drivers.

`compileOnly` mirrors `provided` for annotation processors like Lombok. `testImplementation` and `testRuntimeOnly` cover test-specific needs.

When two dependencies pull different versions of the same library, Gradle resolves conflicts by selecting the **highest requested version** by default. This is safer than Maven's nearest-definition rule, which can silently downgrade a version. For stricter control, `resolutionStrategy.force` pins a specific version, and `strictly` constraints fail the build if any transitive dependency requests a conflicting version.

For managing versions across a multi-module project, version catalogs in `gradle/libs.versions.toml` centralize all coordinates in one file. Every subproject references dependencies as typed accessors like `libs.spring.boot.starter.web`. This replaces the scattered version numbers that drift out of sync when developers copy-paste coordinates between modules. The `platform()` dependency type imports BOMs like Spring Boot's, adopting an entire curated version matrix without declaring individual versions.

sections.title: The implementation vs api Decision in Practice
sections.content:
The distinction between `implementation` and `api` is the single most impactful dependency decision in a Gradle multi-module project. Getting it wrong either leaks internal libraries to consumers or hides types that consumers actually need to compile against.

The rule is straightforward: if a dependency's types appear in your module's public API — in method signatures, return types, or superclass declarations — use `api`. If you only use it internally, use `implementation`. A Spring Boot service module that uses Jackson's `ObjectMapper` internally but only exposes domain objects in its API should declare Jackson as `implementation`, not `api`.

The **compilation speed** impact is measurable. When a module declares a dependency as `implementation` and that dependency's version changes, Gradle only recompiles the declaring module. When it is declared as `api`, Gradle must recompile every module downstream because the dependency is part of the public ABI. On a 30-module project, this difference can turn a 5-second incremental rebuild into a 45-second one.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`implementation` hides dependencies from consumers** — the declaring module can compile and run with it, but downstream modules cannot see it, preventing accidental coupling to internal libraries that may change or be removed
- **`api` exposes dependencies to consumers' compile classpaths** — use only when your public method signatures, return types, or superclass declarations reference the dependency's types directly
- **Highest version wins by default** — unlike Maven's nearest-definition rule which can silently downgrade, Gradle selects the highest requested version, which is generally safer but can still pull breaking major versions
- **Version catalogs in `libs.versions.toml` centralize coordinates** — typed accessors like `libs.spring.boot.starter.web` replace scattered version strings, preventing the drift that happens when developers copy-paste coordinates between modules
- **`platform()` imports BOMs without adding dependencies** — `implementation platform('org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:3.2.0')` adopts Spring's version matrix so individual starters need no explicit version number

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Gradle's dependency management system is built around configurations — named classpaths with specific semantics. The key insight is that `implementation` versus `api` is not just a naming convention; it controls compilation scope and build performance.

**`implementation` vs `api` — the most important distinction**
- `implementation` keeps a dependency internal — downstream modules cannot accidentally import it; changing an `implementation` dependency only recompiles the declaring module
- `api` exposes a dependency publicly — its types appear in the declaring module's public method signatures, and downstream modules can use it; any version change forces recompilation of every downstream module
- The practical rule: default to `implementation` everywhere; switch to `api` only when the compiler tells you a downstream module needs access to the types — overusing `api` defeats the entire configuration system and causes unnecessary recompilation cascades

**Version conflict resolution**
- Gradle's default strategy selects the highest requested version when two dependencies request different versions of the same library — safer than Maven's nearest-definition-wins rule which can silently downgrade
- Version catalogs in `libs.versions.toml` centralize all coordinates in one file — `libs.versions.jackson = "2.16.1"` referenced across all modules ensures consistent versions without duplication
- `resolutionStrategy.force("com.example:library:1.2.3")` pins a specific version regardless of what other dependencies request — use sparingly; it can mask legitimate version conflicts

**Dependency analysis**
- `./gradlew dependencies --configuration runtimeClasspath` shows the full resolved dependency tree for the artifact that ships
- The `com.github.ben-manes.versions` plugin adds `./gradlew dependencyUpdates` which reports which dependencies have newer versions available — useful for regular dependency hygiene

questions.question: What is the Gradle wrapper and why should you use it?
questions.title: The Gradle Wrapper: What It Is and Why to Use It
questions.direct_answer: The Gradle wrapper (`gradlew` / `gradlew.bat`) is a shell script committed to your repository that downloads and runs the exact Gradle version declared in `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`. It ensures every developer and CI machine uses the same Gradle version without requiring a manual installation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the importance of reproducible builds and version pinning in team environments.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running `gradle` directly from a system installation instead of `./gradlew`, which causes builds to break when team members have different Gradle versions installed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention wrapper verification (checking the SHA-256 of the downloaded distribution), using `./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 8.5` to upgrade the wrapper, and that CI systems should always invoke `./gradlew`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Four committed files pin the exact Gradle version** — `gradlew`, `gradlew.bat`, `gradle-wrapper.jar`, and `gradle-wrapper.properties` ensure every developer and CI agent uses identical Gradle binaries with zero manual installation
- **Always invoke `./gradlew`, never bare `gradle`** — running `gradle build` uses whatever version is on `PATH`, reintroducing the exact version inconsistency the wrapper was designed to eliminate
- **`distributionSha256Sum` hardens the supply chain** — the wrapper verifies the downloaded distribution ZIP against this checksum before extracting, catching corrupted or tampered downloads on compromised networks
- **`./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 8.6` upgrades the project** — updates `gradle-wrapper.properties` in one command; commit the change and every teammate picks up the new version automatically on their next build
- **Pre-cache the wrapper in Docker CI images** — bake the Gradle distribution into your CI base image to avoid cold-download latency on every pipeline run, especially behind corporate proxies

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The Gradle wrapper solves the build tool version consistency problem — without it, every developer and CI agent runs whatever version of Gradle they have installed locally, and version mismatches cause builds that work on one machine and fail on another.

**What the wrapper does**
- The wrapper commits a shell script (`gradlew`) and a properties file (`gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`) declaring the exact Gradle version the project uses
- Running `./gradlew build` automatically downloads that version if it is not already cached locally — every developer and every CI agent gets the same binary without manual installation
- The wrapper files are small (a few KB) and should be committed to version control — they are the project's contract with the Gradle version

**Security and upgrade**
- Add `distributionSha256Sum` to the properties file to verify the download integrity — without it, a compromised download mirror could substitute a malicious Gradle binary
- Upgrading is a single command: `./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 8.6` updates the properties file; commit the change and the entire team and CI pick it up automatically on the next build
- Always call `./gradlew`, never bare `gradle` — add a CI lint step that rejects any pipeline script using the system `gradle` command to prevent accidental version drift in automated environments

**Wrapper in CI**
- CI agents do not need Gradle pre-installed — the wrapper handles it; this simplifies CI image management and ensures every project uses its declared version regardless of what other projects on the same agent use

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
The Gradle wrapper (`gradlew` / `gradlew.bat`) is a shell script committed to your repository that downloads and runs the exact Gradle version declared in `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties`.

It ensures every developer and CI machine uses the same Gradle version without requiring a manual installation.

Think of the Gradle wrapper as version pinning for the build tool itself. Your `build.gradle` pins Spring Boot to 3.2.0, your `libs.versions.toml` pins Jackson to 2.16.1 — but without the wrapper, the tool that interprets all of these runs at whatever version each developer happened to install last month. One teammate on Gradle 7.6, another on 8.5, CI on 8.3 — and suddenly a build script that should work everywhere fails on one machine because a deprecated API was removed in a newer version.

Not applying the `io.spring.dependency-management` plugin, which means you have to specify versions for every Spring dependency manually instead of inheriting them from the BOM.

sections.title: Upgrade, Verify, and Enforce the Wrapper Across Your Team
sections.content:
Upgrading the wrapper is a single command: `./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 8.6`. This updates `gradle-wrapper.properties` with the new distribution URL. Commit the changed file and every teammate picks up the new version on their next build — no Slack message, no wiki page, no manual download.

For **supply chain security**, add the `distributionSha256Sum` property to `gradle-wrapper.properties`. The wrapper verifies the downloaded ZIP against this checksum before extracting it, catching corrupted downloads or compromised mirrors. On teams subject to compliance audits, this checksum is evidence that the build toolchain has not been tampered with.

The enforcement piece matters most: lint your CI scripts to reject bare `gradle` invocations and only allow `./gradlew`. A single developer running `gradle build` instead of `./gradlew build` can silently use a different Gradle version, produce different outputs, and introduce failures that nobody else can reproduce. Most teams add a CI check that fails if `gradle-wrapper.jar` is missing from the repository or if any pipeline script uses a bare `gradle` command.

questions.question: How do you configure Gradle for a multi-module project?
questions.title: Configuring Gradle for Multi-Module Projects
questions.direct_answer: A Gradle multi-module project uses `settings.gradle` to declare all subprojects with `include`, a root `build.gradle` for shared configuration applied via `allprojects {}` or `subprojects {}`, and individual subproject `build.gradle` files for module-specific configuration. Modules reference each other as project dependencies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can structure a large codebase into cohesive modules with proper dependency relationships.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `subprojects {}` in the root build to apply plugins, which applies them to every module regardless of type — prefer convention plugins for explicit opt-in.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention composite builds for separating build logic from project builds, using convention plugins in `buildSrc/` to share configuration, and `./gradlew :module:task` syntax for targeted builds.

sections.title: Why a Single build.gradle Becomes Painful at Scale
sections.content:
A Java backend that starts as a single module inevitably grows. The REST controllers, domain logic, persistence layer, and shared utilities all live in one `build.gradle`, one `src/main/java` tree, and one compilation unit. At first this is fine. But once the codebase crosses a few hundred classes, problems compound: changing a repository interface recompiles every controller, test suites run everything on every change, and two developers editing unrelated features create merge conflicts in the same build file.

**A multi-module project** splits the codebase along domain or architectural boundaries. Each module has its own `build.gradle`, its own source tree, and its own dependency declarations. Gradle compiles modules independently and in parallel, so changing the `persistence` module does not trigger recompilation of the `api` module — unless `api` actually depends on `persistence`. The build naturally enforces architectural boundaries that would otherwise be documented but never checked.

The starting point is always `settings.gradle`, which declares which directories are subprojects.

sections.title: Declare Modules in settings.gradle and Wire Dependencies
sections.content:
The `settings.gradle` file is evaluated before any build logic runs. It tells Gradle which directories contain subprojects. Each module listed here must have its own `build.gradle` file.

```groovy
// settings.gradle
rootProject.name = 'order-system'
include 'domain'
include 'persistence'
include 'service'
include 'web'
```

Modules reference each other as `project(':name')` dependencies. Gradle reads these references, builds a dependency graph, and compiles modules in topological order. If `service` depends on `domain`, Gradle compiles `domain` first regardless of declaration order in `settings.gradle`.

```groovy
// service/build.gradle
plugins { id 'java-library' }
dependencies {
    implementation project(':domain')
    implementation project(':persistence')
}
```

The `implementation` keyword means `domain` and `persistence` are internal to `service`. Modules that depend on `service` cannot transitively see `domain` classes unless `service` declares them with `api` instead.

sections.title: Use Convention Plugins Instead of subprojects{} for Shared Configuration
Build Only What Changed With Targeted Task Execution
sections.content:
The primary developer experience advantage of a Gradle multi-module project is targeted execution. Running `./gradlew :service:test` compiles and tests only the `service` module plus any upstream dependencies that need rebuilding. Gradle's incremental build system ensures that if `domain` was already compiled and its sources have not changed, it is skipped.

For CI pipelines, `./gradlew build --parallel` builds independent modules concurrently. On a project with 10 modules where only 3 are in the dependency chain, the remaining 7 build in parallel. The `--build-cache` flag, enabled by default since Gradle 7, restores outputs from previous builds, so clean CI checkouts still benefit from cached compilation.

The key production mistake to avoid is **circular dependencies** between modules. Gradle detects and rejects them immediately, unlike runtime frameworks that might silently tolerate them. Structure modules so that dependencies flow in one direction — domain has no dependencies, persistence depends on domain, service depends on both. This unidirectional flow keeps the dependency graph acyclic and makes build ordering deterministic.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`settings.gradle` declares the project structure** — `include` lists every subproject that Gradle manages; modules not listed are invisible to the build and cannot be referenced as `project(':name')` dependencies
- **Convention plugins replace `subprojects {}`** — define shared Java toolchain, test framework, and linter configuration in `buildSrc/` and apply per-module, so non-Java modules are not forced to inherit JVM plugin settings
- **`project(':name')` dependencies enforce build order** — Gradle resolves inter-module references and compiles in topological order; cycles are detected and rejected immediately, naturally enforcing architectural boundaries
- **Targeted execution saves rebuild time** — `./gradlew :service:test` compiles and tests only the target module and its upstream dependencies, skipping unrelated modules entirely during development
- **`implementation` vs `api` controls module coupling** — declaring `project(':domain')` as `implementation` prevents downstream modules from transitively accessing domain classes through the declaring module's classpath

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A multi-module Gradle project uses `settings.gradle` to define the project structure and convention plugins to share configuration without the brittle `subprojects {}` pattern.

**Project structure and discovery**
- `settings.gradle` includes each subproject with `include(':api', ':service', ':domain')` — Gradle reads this file first and builds the project tree before any build logic runs
- Subprojects reference each other with `dependencies { implementation project(':domain') }` — Gradle builds a dependency graph from these references and compiles in the correct order automatically
- Targeted execution: `./gradlew :service:test` rebuilds only what that module needs — the domain module compiles if it is a dependency, unrelated modules are skipped

**Convention plugins over `subprojects {}`**
- `subprojects {}` in the root build applies settings to every module blindly — a module that needs different behavior requires special-casing with `if (project.name == ...)`, which becomes unmaintainable
- Convention plugins in `buildSrc/` are Kotlin or Groovy files that each module explicitly applies: `apply plugin: 'com.example.java-conventions'` — the module opts in to shared toolchain, test framework, and dependency management configuration
- Different module types apply different convention plugins — an API module applies `java-library-conventions`, a Spring Boot application applies `spring-boot-conventions`; the conventions encode the team's standards once and modules consume them

**When to start with convention plugins**
- Start with convention plugins from day one, not `subprojects {}` — migrating later requires touching every module's build file and is the most common source of inconsistency in multi-module Gradle projects
- Use `dependencyResolutionManagement` in `settings.gradle` for the version catalog — centralizing coordinates there makes them available to all modules without each module importing the catalog separately

questions.question: How does Gradle incremental build work?
questions.title: Gradle Incremental Build: How It Works
questions.direct_answer: Gradle tracks the declared inputs and outputs of every task. Before executing a task it computes fingerprints of those files and properties and compares them to the previous run. If nothing has changed, the task is marked UP-TO-DATE and skipped entirely, saving build time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand how Gradle achieves faster repeated builds and what conditions break incremental behavior.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not annotating custom task inputs and outputs, which means Gradle cannot track changes and always re-runs the task, defeating incremental build.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish between up-to-date checks (local, per-task) and the build cache (distributable, shared across machines and CI), and mention that the configuration cache is a separate optimization at the configuration phase level.

sections.title: Why Gradle Rebuilds in Seconds What Takes Minutes From Scratch
sections.content:
Most build tools execute every task on every run. You type `mvn package` and Maven dutifully compiles, tests, and packages even if you changed nothing since the last build. Gradle takes a fundamentally different approach: before executing any task, it checks whether the work has already been done. If a task's inputs and outputs have not changed since the last successful run, Gradle prints `UP-TO-DATE` and skips it entirely.

This is not a simple timestamp check. **Gradle fingerprints every declared input and output** — file contents are hashed, property values are recorded, and the aggregate fingerprint is stored in the project's `.gradle/` directory. On the next build, Gradle recomputes the fingerprints and compares them. A single changed source file in a 500-file module triggers recompilation of that module, but every other module whose inputs are unchanged is skipped in milliseconds.

The mechanism has three layers that build on each other: input/output fingerprinting, the up-to-date check, and the build cache. Understanding each layer explains why Gradle builds get faster over time rather than slower.

sections.title: Input and Output Fingerprinting: How Gradle Knows What Changed
sections.content:
Every Gradle task declares its **inputs** and **outputs** through annotated properties. The `compileJava` task declares source files as `@InputFiles`, the classpath as `@Classpath`, and compiler arguments as `@Input` properties. Its outputs are the compiled `.class` files in the build directory, declared as `@OutputDirectory`. Gradle hashes the content of every input file and records the value of every input property.

After a task executes successfully, Gradle stores these fingerprints in the `.gradle/` directory. Before the next execution, it recomputes the fingerprints and compares them to the stored values. If every input fingerprint matches and every output file still exists with the same content, the task is marked `UP-TO-DATE` and skipped.

The fingerprinting is **content-based, not timestamp-based**. Touching a file without changing its contents does not invalidate the fingerprint. Checking out a branch that has the same source files with different timestamps still produces cache hits. This distinction matters in CI where builds start from a clean checkout — timestamps change on every clone, but content hashes remain stable.

sections.title: The UP-TO-DATE Check: Skipping Work in Milliseconds
sections.content:
When Gradle evaluates a task during execution, it runs the up-to-date check before calling the task's action. The check compares current input fingerprints against stored fingerprints from the last successful execution. If everything matches, Gradle prints the task name with `UP-TO-DATE` and moves to the next task in the graph. No class files are generated, no tests run, no JARs are packaged.

The speed of this check is what makes Gradle's incremental build practical. Computing a content hash of a source file takes microseconds. Comparing stored fingerprints is an in-memory operation. On a 50-module project where you changed one file in one module, Gradle checks and skips 49 modules' `compileJava` tasks in under a second, then recompiles only the changed module.

**Custom tasks participate in this system only if they declare their inputs and outputs.** A task without `@Input` and `@Output` annotations has no fingerprints to compare, so Gradle either always runs it or never detects that it is stale. This is the most common reason teams see `Task :generateConfig EXECUTED` on every build — the task is missing annotations.

sections.title: The Build Cache: Sharing Skipped Work Across Machines
sections.content:
The up-to-date check only works locally — it compares against fingerprints from the last execution on this machine. The **build cache** extends this concept across machines and across time. When a task executes, Gradle stores its outputs in a cache keyed by a hash of all inputs. When any machine encounters a task with the same input hash, it pulls the outputs from the cache instead of re-executing.

The local cache lives in `~/.gradle/caches/`. A remote cache — backed by an HTTP server, Gradle Enterprise, or a cloud bucket — makes this work across the team. A CI build compiles the `domain` module with inputs A and stores the result. A developer who later pulls the same branch has inputs A and retrieves the compiled output from the remote cache in milliseconds instead of compiling locally.

The build cache requires tasks to produce **deterministic outputs**. Timestamps embedded in generated files, random UUIDs in file names, or non-reproducible line ordering break cache hits because the stored output hash would never match a recomputed one. Task authors must use `@CacheableTask` and ensure all outputs are reproducible for cache entries to be reusable.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Content-based hashing, not timestamps** — Gradle fingerprints file contents and property values, so touching a file without changing it or checking out a branch with different timestamps does not invalidate the cache
- **Custom tasks must declare `@Input` and `@Output`** — without annotations Gradle has no fingerprints to compare, so the task either always re-executes or never detects stale outputs, defeating incremental build entirely
- **UP-TO-DATE is local, build cache is distributed** — the up-to-date check compares against the last local execution; the build cache stores outputs keyed by input hashes and serves them to any machine with matching inputs
- **`@CacheableTask` requires deterministic outputs** — timestamps, random UUIDs, or non-reproducible ordering in generated files break cache hits because the stored output hash will never match a recomputed one
- **`--info` diagnoses why a task re-executed** — Gradle logs which specific input or output changed, which is essential for debugging unexpected rebuilds caused by missing annotations or non-deterministic outputs

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Gradle's incremental build is the reason Gradle feels faster than Maven on repeated builds — it treats every task as a pure function and skips re-execution when nothing changed.

**How UP-TO-DATE checking works**
- Before running any task, Gradle hashes all declared inputs — source files, configuration values, classpath entries — and compares the hash to the stored fingerprint from the last successful execution
- If every input hash matches, the task is marked `UP-TO-DATE` and skipped entirely — the output from the previous execution is reused
- Content-based, not timestamp-based: touching a file without changing its content does not trigger a rebuild; this distinction matters in CI where every `git checkout` produces fresh timestamps but identical source files

**The build cache — sharing outputs across machines**
- When a task runs, Gradle stores its outputs keyed by input hash in the build cache — local by default, shared with a remote cache server optionally
- A developer whose input hash matches a task CI already ran pulls the cached output instead of recompiling — a 30-second compile task takes under 200 milliseconds from cache
- Enable remote cache with `buildCache { remote(HttpBuildCache) { url = 'https://your-cache/cache/'; push = System.getenv('CI') != null } }` — only CI pushes to the cache; developers only pull

**Custom task annotation requirements**
- Custom tasks without `@Input` and `@OutputDirectory` annotations on their properties re-execute on every build — Gradle cannot determine what changed if inputs and outputs are not declared
- The symptom: a custom task always shows `EXECUTED` instead of `UP-TO-DATE`; run with `--info` to see which input Gradle detected as changed
- Use `@InputFiles`, `@InputDirectory`, `@OutputFile`, `@Internal` precisely — over-declaring inputs causes false cache misses; under-declaring causes stale output to be used incorrectly
